title: Communism in Power
bigQuestion: Why did a movement that promised equality and an end to exploitation produce some of the deadliest governments of the twentieth century?

story.title: The Last of the Grain
story.kicker: In the fall of 1932 a farmer in Soviet Ukraine watches officials search his house for food.
paragraphs: Picture a village in central Ukraine in November 1932. A farmer we will call Mykola stands in his yard with his wife and two children. A few years earlier the family worked its own fields. Now the land belongs to the collective farm. Mykola works there with his neighbors, and the state decides how much grain the farm must hand over.

The quota this year is far too high. The harvest was poor, and the farm cannot meet it. So a brigade of officials and local activists goes from house to house. They carry long metal rods. They push the rods into the dirt floors and the walls, feeling for hidden sacks. They take the grain Mykola saved for winter. Then they take the beans and the dried peas.

Mykola is not a rich man. He owns one cow and a small garden. But the officials call anyone who hides food a saboteur, an enemy of the people. A new law allows long prison terms, or even death, for taking grain from collective fields. People call it the law of five ears of wheat, because gleaning a handful could bring a heavy sentence.

That winter and spring, hunger spread across Ukraine. Villages that failed their quotas were put on blacklists and cut off from goods. In January 1933 the government also stopped most peasants from leaving Ukraine to look for food. Millions of people died. Ukrainians today call this the Holodomor, which means death by hunger.

Mykola lived under a government that said it spoke for workers and peasants. Its leaders believed they were building a fair society with no rich and no poor. This chapter asks how that dream turned into the scene in Mykola's yard.
story.think: The officials in the story believed, or said they believed, that they were serving a just cause. What makes it possible for ordinary people to carry out orders that cause great harm?

sections.title: From an Idea to a Revolution

lessons.title: Marx's Promise
lessons.mainIdea: Karl Marx argued that history is a struggle between classes and that workers would one day overthrow owners and share all property.
reading: In the 1840s Karl Marx, a German writer, lived in cities full of new factories. He saw children working long shifts and families crowded into one room. Factory owners grew rich, while workers earned barely enough to eat. Marx asked why a world that made so much wealth left so many people poor.

His answer was *class struggle*. Marx said every society splits into groups based on who owns the means of production, such as land, mines and factories. In his day, owners formed the bourgeoisie. The workers who sold their labor formed the *proletariat*. Marx believed owners kept part of the value workers made, and he called this exploitation.

Marx predicted that workers would rise up, take the factories and share them. In time, he wrote, a *communist* society would have no classes, no private ownership of factories and, in the end, no need for a state at all. Supporters saw a vision of justice. Critics said it ignored human nature and gave no plan for protecting freedom along the way.

words.d: Marx's idea that history is driven by conflict between groups that own property and groups that work for them
in Marx's writing, the working class who sell their labor for wages
describing a society, or a movement toward one, where property is shared in common and classes disappear

look.title: The Opening Claim of the Manifesto
look.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
look.cite: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848), English translation by Samuel Moore, 1888
look.prompt: Put this sentence in your own words. What does Marx think is the main force that shapes history?

check.q: What did Marx call the working class who sell their labor for wages?
check.why: In Marx's writing the proletariat are wage workers; the bourgeoisie are the owners.

check.q: According to the reading, what problem was Marx trying to explain?
choices: Why factories made great wealth while many workers stayed poor
Why kings lost power to elected parliaments
Why farming spread from the Middle East to Europe
Why Germany had many small states
check.why: The reading says Marx asked why a world that made so much wealth left so many people poor.

check.q: What was one criticism of Marx's vision named in the reading?
choices: It gave no plan for protecting freedom along the way
It praised factory owners too much
It said classes could never disappear
It was written only for farmers
check.why: Critics said Marx ignored human nature and gave no plan for protecting freedom during the change.

lessons.title: Lenin and the Revolution of 1917
lessons.mainIdea: In 1917 Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Russia and began building a state run by one party in the name of the workers.
reading: In early 1917 Russia was losing badly in World War I. Bread lines stretched through the capital, Petrograd. Workers and soldiers rebelled, and Tsar Nicholas II gave up his throne in March. A temporary government took over, but it kept fighting the war and could not end the hunger.

Vladimir Lenin led a small, disciplined party called the Bolsheviks. Lenin added a key idea to Marx. He said workers would not rise up on their own. They needed a *vanguard party* of full-time revolutionaries to lead them. This blend of ideas became known as *Marxism-Leninism*. In November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized power with the slogan Peace, Land and Bread.

Lenin's government soon shut down rival parties and newspapers. It closed an elected assembly in January 1918 after the Bolsheviks failed to win a majority in it. A secret police called the Cheka arrested and shot opponents. A brutal civil war followed until about 1921. In 1922 the new state was named the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, or USSR. Supporters saw a workers' victory. Critics saw a new dictatorship.

words.d: Lenin's idea of a small group of dedicated revolutionaries who lead the working class
Marx's ideas combined with Lenin's plan for rule by a single revolutionary party
Lenin's party, which took power in Russia in November 1917 and later became the Communist Party

look.title: Two Views of November 1917
look.text: A Bolshevik factory worker says: For the first time, people like me run the country. The war will end and the land will go to those who farm it. A Russian voter says: I voted in the assembly election. When the Bolsheviks lost, they closed the assembly with soldiers. Who decides for the workers now?
look.prompt: What does each speaker value most? Using the reading, explain which facts support each view.

check.q: What was Lenin's idea of a vanguard party?
choices: A small group of dedicated revolutionaries who lead the workers
An army that guards the border
A party that shares power with the tsar
check.why: Lenin said workers needed a vanguard party of full-time revolutionaries to lead them.

check.q: What slogan did the Bolsheviks use in 1917?
check.why: The Bolsheviks promised Peace, Land and Bread to war-weary, hungry Russians.

check.q: What did Lenin's government do after it failed to win a majority in the elected assembly?
choices: It handed power to the winners
check.why: The reading says the Bolsheviks closed the elected assembly in January 1918.

lessons.title: One Party and Collective Farms
lessons.mainIdea: Under Stalin, one party controlled all of Soviet life and forced peasants onto collective farms at a terrible cost.
reading: After Lenin died in 1924, Joseph Stalin outmaneuvered his rivals. By about 1929 he held nearly total power. The Communist Party was the only legal party. It ran the government, the army, the newspapers, the schools and the unions. A system in which one party rules and no rival is allowed is called a *one-party state*.

Stalin wanted to turn a farming country into an industrial power fast. His Five-Year Plans built steel mills, dams and whole new cities. To feed the workers and sell grain abroad, he forced peasants to give up their own plots and join *collective farms*. The state set what they grew and how much they handed over.

Many peasants resisted. Some slaughtered their animals rather than give them up. Stalin blamed better-off farmers, called kulaks, and ordered them removed as a class. Well over a million people were deported to remote regions. Soviet factories grew quickly, and supporters pointed to that growth. Critics point to the hunger, the lost freedom and the lives it cost.

words.d: a country where only one political party is allowed to exist and rule
large farms owned or controlled by the state, where peasants worked together and handed over set amounts of their harvest
the Soviet label for better-off peasants, used to target them for arrest and deportation

look.title: A Five-Year Plan Poster in Words
look.text: Picture a bright Soviet poster from about 1930. A smiling worker stands in front of smoking factory chimneys and a new tractor. Big red letters promise to finish the Five-Year Plan in four years. There are no hungry villages in the picture.
look.prompt: What does this poster want viewers to feel? What does it leave out, based on the reading?

check.q: What is a one-party state?
choices: A country where only one party is allowed to exist and rule
A country with two parties that take turns
A country ruled by a king and a parliament
check.why: A one-party state allows no rival parties; in the USSR only the Communist Party was legal.

check.q: Why did Stalin force peasants onto collective farms?
choices: To control grain to feed workers and sell abroad for rapid industry
To give each peasant family more land of its own
To return land to the old nobles
check.why: The reading says collectivization aimed to feed workers and earn money for fast industrial growth.

check.q: Who were the kulaks in Soviet language?
choices: Better-off peasants targeted for arrest and deportation
check.why: Kulak was the label for better-off peasants, whom Stalin ordered removed as a class.

lessons.title: The Holodomor
lessons.mainIdea: In 1932 and 1933 Soviet grain policies caused a famine in Ukraine that killed millions of people.
reading: Collectivization disrupted farming across the USSR, and hunger struck several regions, including Kazakhstan. In Ukraine the famine of 1932 and 1933 was especially deadly. Grain quotas stayed high even as people starved. Brigades searched homes and took seed grain and other food, as in the chapter's opening story.

Several policies made things worse. Villages that missed quotas were blacklisted and cut off from stores. In January 1933 most peasants were barred from leaving Ukraine to find food. Meanwhile the USSR kept exporting grain. Scholars estimate that roughly 3.5 to 5 million people died in Ukraine. Ukrainians call the famine the *Holodomor*, death by hunger.

Historians still debate one question. Was the famine a deliberate *genocide* aimed at Ukrainians as a nation, or a crime of brutal policy aimed at peasants everywhere? Ukraine and many other countries, including the United States, have officially called it a genocide. Some historians stress Stalin's fear of Ukrainian nationalism. Others stress the wider war on the peasantry. All agree the deaths were caused by human decisions.

words.d: the famine in Soviet Ukraine in 1932 and 1933, whose name means death by hunger
acts carried out to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group
a fixed amount that must be produced or handed over

look.title: Two Historians Disagree
look.text: Historian A: The rules that trapped peasants inside Ukraine and the blacklists on villages show the famine targeted Ukrainians as a people. Historian B: Peasants also starved in Kazakhstan and southern Russia. Stalin's war was against the peasantry as a class, and Ukraine suffered most because it grew the most grain.
look.prompt: Which facts from the reading does each historian use? What further evidence would help you judge between them?

check.q: What does the word Holodomor mean?
check.why: Holodomor is the Ukrainian name for the 1932 to 1933 famine and means death by hunger.

check.q: Which policy in the reading kept starving Ukrainian peasants from finding food elsewhere?
choices: A ban on most peasants leaving Ukraine in January 1933
A rule that all grain be sold to Poland
A law giving each family a new cow
A plan to move factories into Ukraine
check.why: The reading says most peasants were barred from leaving Ukraine to look for food.

check.q: What question about the Holodomor do historians still debate?
choices: Whether it was a genocide aimed at Ukrainians as a nation or a wider war on peasants
Whether any people died at all
Whether it happened in the 1800s or the 1900s
Whether it was caused by a volcano
check.why: The debate is over intent; all agree human decisions caused the deaths.

lessons.title: The Gulag and the Great Terror
lessons.mainIdea: Stalin's regime sent millions to labor camps and, in 1937 and 1938, executed hundreds of thousands of people it called enemies.
reading: The *Gulag* was the Soviet system of forced labor camps. Prisoners cut timber, dug canals and mined gold in freezing places such as Kolyma in the far northeast. Many had done nothing a free country would call a crime. A joke about Stalin, a late arrival at work or a relative abroad could be enough.

In 1937 and 1938 the arrests became a flood called the *Great Terror*. The secret police, then called the NKVD, worked from quotas of enemies to find in each region. Old Bolsheviks confessed to wild charges at public *show trials*. Army officers, engineers, poets and ordinary workers were arrested. Soviet records later showed that roughly 680,000 people were shot in those two years.

Writers who survived told the world. Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, a former prisoner, described camp life in One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, published in 1962. Later he wrote The Gulag Archipelago. After the USSR opened its archives around 1991, historians confirmed much of what survivors had said.

words.d: the Soviet system of forced labor camps, from a Russian abbreviation for the camp administration
Stalin's wave of mass arrests and executions in 1937 and 1938
public trials where the verdict is decided in advance and the accused are pressured to confess

look.title: The Scale of Stalin's Repression (rounded)
rows: People who passed through the Gulag, 1930-53
look.cite: Anne Applebaum, Gulag: A History, 2003; Soviet archival figures cited by historians
look.prompt: Which number is largest? Why might a camp system that held many people at once still be smaller than the total who passed through it?

check.q: What was the Gulag?
choices: The Soviet system of forced labor camps
check.why: The Gulag was the network of forced labor camps, such as those at Kolyma.

check.q: What happened at a show trial?
choices: The verdict was decided in advance and the accused were pushed to confess
A jury of workers freely weighed the evidence
check.why: Show trials were staged for the public with the outcome fixed beforehand.

check.q: How did historians confirm survivors' accounts of the camps?
choices: They studied Soviet archives opened around 1991
They relied only on Stalin's speeches
They counted votes from Soviet elections
check.why: The reading says the archives opened around 1991 confirmed much of what survivors reported.

lessons.title: Mao and the Great Leap Forward
lessons.mainIdea: Mao Zedong's Great Leap Forward tried to transform China overnight and caused the deadliest famine in recorded history.
reading: Mao Zedong's Communist Party won China's civil war in 1949. Many peasants welcomed land reform, which took land from landlords and gave it to poor farmers. The reform was also violent. Large numbers of landlords were killed at village meetings. Within a few years, the land was pooled again into collectives.

In 1958 Mao launched the *Great Leap Forward*. He wanted China to pass Britain in steel output within about fifteen years. Villages were merged into huge *people's communes*. Families ate in shared canteens. Millions of peasants left the fields to melt pots and tools in small backyard furnaces. Much of the iron they made was useless.

Local officials, afraid of punishment, reported record harvests that did not exist. The state took grain based on those false numbers. From 1959 to 1961, famine swept the countryside. Scholars' estimates of the deaths range from about 15 million to 45 million, and many cite around 30 million. When the defense minister, Peng Dehuai, raised concerns in 1959, Mao purged him.

words.d: Mao's 1958 to 1962 campaign to speed up farming and industry in China, which caused a massive famine
very large rural units in Mao's China that combined many villages and controlled work, food and daily life
taking land from large owners and giving it to farmers who work it

look.title: Estimates of Deaths in the Great Leap Famine
look.cite: Banister, China's Changing Population, 1987; Yang, Tombstone, 2008; Dikotter, Mao's Great Famine, 2010
look.prompt: Why might careful scholars reach different totals? What do all three estimates agree on?

check.q: What was a people's commune?
choices: A huge rural unit that joined many villages and controlled work and food
A city council elected by voters
A factory owned by a foreign company
check.why: Communes merged villages and ran daily life, including shared canteens.

check.q: Why did the state take too much grain during the Great Leap?
choices: Officials reported false record harvests out of fear
Peasants voted to give away their grain
A war with Britain cut off food
China had no farms at the time
check.why: The reading says frightened officials inflated harvests, and grain was taken based on those numbers.

check.q: What happened to Peng Dehuai when he raised concerns in 1959?
choices: He was made head of the communes
He was sent to study in Moscow as a reward
check.why: Mao removed the defense minister for criticizing the campaign.

lessons.title: The Cultural Revolution
lessons.mainIdea: From 1966 Mao urged young Red Guards to attack teachers, officials and old traditions, throwing China into a decade of turmoil.
reading: Picture a middle school in Beijing in 1966. Students paste large handwritten posters on the walls accusing their teachers of being enemies of the revolution. Some teachers are forced to wear dunce caps and are beaten. A few are killed. This was the start of the *Cultural Revolution*, which lasted until Mao's death in 1976.

Mao, sidelined after the Great Leap, wanted to regain control and keep the revolution alive. He called on young *Red Guards* to smash the Four Olds: old customs, culture, habits and ideas. They wrecked temples, burned books and paraded officials in public *struggle sessions*, where a person was shouted at, humiliated and forced to confess.

A *cult of personality* surrounded Mao. Millions carried his Little Red Book of quotations. Schools and universities closed for years. Millions of city youths were later sent to the countryside to learn from peasants. Deaths are estimated in the hundreds of thousands at least, and some scholars estimate far more. China's later leaders officially called the period a grave mistake.

words.d: Mao's 1966 to 1976 campaign to purge rivals and old ways of thinking, which caused widespread violence
young people who answered Mao's call to attack enemies of the revolution
public meetings where a person was humiliated and forced to confess to political crimes
the use of propaganda to present a leader as heroic, wise and beyond criticism

look.title: A Student's Choice
look.text: You are fifteen in 1966. Your class is writing a poster that accuses your math teacher of being a class enemy. She once gave you extra help after school. Everyone is watching to see whether you sign. Refusing could mark you as an enemy too.
look.prompt: What pressures does this student face? How does this scene help explain why ordinary people took part in the Cultural Revolution?

check.q: What were the Four Olds that Red Guards attacked?
choices: Old customs, culture, habits and ideas
Old farms, factories, mines and railroads
Old kings, priests, soldiers and judges
Old books, songs, maps and coins only
check.why: Mao told Red Guards to smash old customs, culture, habits and ideas.

check.q: What is a cult of personality?
choices: Propaganda that presents a leader as heroic and beyond criticism
A religious group that rejects all leaders
A vote to remove a leader
check.why: The Little Red Book and endless praise of Mao are examples of a cult of personality.

check.q: How did China's later leaders officially describe the Cultural Revolution?
check.why: The reading says China's later leaders officially called it a grave mistake.

lessons.title: The Khmer Rouge in Cambodia
lessons.mainIdea: From 1975 to 1979 the Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities and killed or starved about 1.5 to 2 million people.
reading: On April 17, 1975, Khmer Rouge soldiers entered Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia. Within days they ordered the whole city, well over a million people, to march into the countryside. The sick were pushed out of hospitals. The new rulers, led by Pol Pot, declared Year Zero, a complete break with the past.

The Khmer Rouge wanted a pure society of peasants with no money, markets, schools or religion. People worked on farms from dawn to night under guard. Teachers, doctors, monks, people who wore glasses and ethnic minorities such as Vietnamese and Cham Muslims were targeted. Mass graves later found across the country became known as the *killing fields*.

At a former school in Phnom Penh called S-21, or Tuol Sleng, thousands of prisoners were photographed, tortured and killed. Scholars estimate that about 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians died from execution, starvation, overwork and disease. That was roughly a fifth of the population. The regime fell when Vietnam invaded in January 1979. It is widely described as an *autogenocide*, a people destroyed by rulers from its own nation.

words.d: the Communist movement led by Pol Pot that ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1979
the mass grave sites across Cambodia where the Khmer Rouge buried its victims
a term for mass killing carried out by a government against large parts of its own people

look.title: Cambodia Under the Khmer Rouge (rounded)
look.unit: million people; years in power in years
look.cite: Ben Kiernan, The Pol Pot Regime, 1996; Yale University Cambodian Genocide Program
look.prompt: About what share of the population died? Show how you worked it out.

check.q: What did the Khmer Rouge do right after taking Phnom Penh?
choices: Forced the whole city to march into the countryside
check.why: The reading says the whole city was ordered into the countryside within days.

check.q: Which groups did the Khmer Rouge target, according to the reading?
choices: Teachers, doctors, monks and ethnic minorities
Only members of the Khmer Rouge
Only people who lived in Vietnam
check.why: Educated people, monks and minorities like the Cham were singled out.

check.q: How did Khmer Rouge rule end?
choices: The United Nations bought the country
Cambodian peasants voted it out in 1975
check.why: The regime fell when Vietnamese forces invaded in January 1979.

lessons.title: Cuba and North Korea
lessons.mainIdea: Communist governments still rule in Cuba and North Korea, each with its own history of promises and repression.
reading: In 1959 Fidel Castro's rebels overthrew Cuba's dictator, Fulgencio Batista. Castro soon declared the revolution socialist and allied with the USSR. His government expanded schooling and free health care, and it ran a large literacy campaign in 1961. Supporters still point to these gains.

Castro's Cuba also became a one-party state. Independent newspapers were closed, and critics were jailed. Private businesses were taken over. Well over a million Cubans have left the island since 1959, many for Florida. Critics describe a country where people lack free speech and free elections.

North Korea was founded in 1948 under Kim Il Sung. His son and grandson have ruled since. The state teaches *Juche*, or self-reliance, and surrounds the Kim family with a cult of personality. A famine in the 1990s killed hundreds of thousands of people, by many estimates. A United Nations inquiry in 2014 reported vast political prison camps. North Korea is often called the most closed country on earth.

words.d: North Korea's official idea of national self-reliance
an organized effort to teach large numbers of people to read and write
a ruler with total power who is not limited by elections or courts

look.title: A United Nations Finding
look.text: The inquiry found that North Korea commits systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations, including a network of political prison camps, on a scale without parallel in the modern world.
look.cite: United Nations Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, Report, 2014 (summary)
look.prompt: What kind of evidence would a commission need to reach this finding about a closed country? Why might that be hard to gather?

check.q: Whom did Fidel Castro's rebels overthrow in 1959?
check.why: Castro's rebels overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista.

check.q: What does Juche mean in North Korea?
check.why: Juche is North Korea's official idea of national self-reliance.

check.q: Which gain do supporters of Cuba's government point to?
choices: Expanded schooling and free health care
check.why: The reading names schooling, free health care and the 1961 literacy campaign.

lessons.title: Why People Were Drawn to It
lessons.mainIdea: Communism attracted people with real hopes for equality, land and dignity, even as its record in power turned out very differently.
reading: Imagine a landless farmworker in China in the 1940s. He pays half his crop to a landlord and owes money he can never repay. A Communist organizer arrives and promises land of his own. For people like him, the offer was powerful. Communism spoke to real suffering.

Across the world, communism promised *equality*, an end to *exploitation*, jobs for all and freedom from foreign rule. In colonies, it offered a way to fight empires. In the 1930s, when capitalist countries sank into the Great Depression, the USSR claimed to have no unemployment. Some Western writers visited and praised it, often without seeing the famines.

In power, the pattern was often the same. A single party claimed to know the one true path. Anyone who disagreed became an enemy. With no free press, courts or elections to check them, leaders made disastrous choices and no one could stop them. Defenders of socialist ideas argue that these regimes betrayed Marx's goals. Critics argue that concentrating all economic and political power made abuse likely.

words.d: the state of people having the same rights, status or share
unfairly using someone's work for another person's gain
limits, such as courts, elections and a free press, that stop leaders from abusing power

look.title: Promise and Record
look.text: Promise: land for peasants. Record: land taken back into collectives and communes. Promise: power to the workers. Record: power held by one party and its leader. Promise: an end to hunger. Record: the Holodomor and the Great Leap famine.
look.prompt: Pick one pair. Using facts from the chapter, explain why the promise and the record came apart.

check.q: Why did communism appeal to many landless farmworkers?
choices: It promised them land of their own
It promised to keep landlords in charge
It promised to end all farming
check.why: The reading's example is a farmworker drawn by the promise of his own land.

check.q: Why did the USSR look attractive to some people in the 1930s?
choices: It claimed to have no unemployment during the Great Depression
It held free elections every year
It had the world's largest navy
check.why: When capitalist countries faced mass unemployment, the USSR claimed full employment.

check.q: What argument do critics make about why these regimes turned abusive?
choices: Concentrating all economic and political power made abuse likely
They had too many political parties
Their newspapers criticized leaders too much
check.why: Critics say that with no checks on concentrated power, abuse became likely.

lessons.title: The Wall Falls
lessons.mainIdea: In 1989 the Berlin Wall fell and Eastern European communist governments collapsed; in 1991 the Soviet Union itself broke apart.
reading: On the night of November 9, 1989, East German officials announced, by mistake, that their citizens could cross the border freely. Crowds rushed to the *Berlin Wall*, which had divided the city since 1961. Guards opened the gates. People climbed on the wall and chipped pieces off with hammers.

The fall came after years of pressure. Mikhail Gorbachev, the Soviet leader from 1985, allowed more open talk, called *glasnost*, and tried economic reform. In Poland the Solidarity trade union, led by Lech Walesa, won partly free elections in 1989. That year communist rule ended across Eastern Europe, mostly without bloodshed. Romania was the violent exception.

In 1991 the USSR broke into fifteen independent countries, including Russia, Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The Soviet flag came down over the Kremlin on December 25. China's Communist Party kept power, but it crushed the Tiananmen Square protests in June 1989 and later opened its economy to markets. The Cold War contest between communism and the West was over.

words.d: the guarded wall that divided East and West Berlin from 1961 to 1989
Gorbachev's policy of greater openness and freer discussion in the USSR
the independent Polish trade union that led peaceful opposition to communist rule

look.title: Two Crowds in 1989
look.text: In November, a crowd in Berlin climbs the wall while guards stand aside. In June, a crowd of students in Beijing's Tiananmen Square is cleared by tanks and soldiers. Both crowds wanted more freedom.
look.prompt: Why might the two events have ended so differently? Use at least one fact from the reading.

check.q: What was glasnost?
check.why: Glasnost was Gorbachev's policy of freer discussion.

check.q: Which Eastern European country's change in 1989 was violent, according to the reading?
check.why: The reading calls Romania the violent exception.

check.q: What happened to the USSR in 1991?
choices: It broke into fifteen independent countries
check.why: The USSR dissolved into fifteen countries, and its flag came down on December 25, 1991.

review.q: Which idea did Lenin add to Marx's theory?
choices: A vanguard party of revolutionaries must lead the workers
review.why: Lenin's vanguard party idea is the core of Marxism-Leninism.

choices: The 1932 to 1933 famine in Soviet Ukraine
review.why: The Holodomor was the famine in Ukraine caused by Soviet grain policies.

choices: Great Leap Forward and Mao Zedong
review.why: Mao launched the Great Leap; the Terror was Stalin's, Year Zero Pol Pot's and Juche North Korea's.

choices: Life in the Soviet labor camps
The fall of the Berlin Wall
review.why: Solzhenitsyn, a former prisoner, wrote about the Gulag.

review.q: How did the Khmer Rouge regime differ from Castro's Cuba?
choices: It abolished money and schools and killed about a fifth of the population
It expanded schooling and health care
It allied with the United States
review.why: The Khmer Rouge abolished money, schools and religion; Cuba expanded schooling while limiting freedom.

review.q: What common pattern does the chapter find in communist states in power?
choices: One party claimed the true path and removed all checks on its power
review.why: With no press, courts or elections to check them, leaders' disastrous choices went unstopped.

review.q: Which fact about the Great Leap famine do all scholars in the chapter agree on?
choices: Tens of millions of people died
review.why: Estimates range from about 15 to 45 million, but all show a catastrophic toll.

review.q: What happened on the night of November 9, 1989?
choices: Crowds crossed the Berlin Wall after the border was opened
Khmer Rouge soldiers entered Phnom Penh
review.why: An announcement opened the border, and crowds crossed the Berlin Wall.
